maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I addressed the committee on Tuesday I had completed a portion of my remarks but had not given all the information to which I think hon. members are entitled. I had given a review of the operations of the Royal Canadian Air Force during the past year. I should like now to take some of the time of the committee to develop our plans for the future, and, following a custom which seems to have met with favour, to give an account of what might be described as headaches which confront us in dealing with matters intimately connected with the Royal Canadian Air Force.
I propose to deai to-day with the questions of repatriation and demobilization, and, without entering upon the sphere of rehabilitation -which I hope to show is not within the jurisdiction of the defence departments-to give some idea of the plans and blueprints
we have in mind, while at the same time explaining to the committee some of the difficulties we must make up our minds to meet. If I ipay, I would ask hon. members to consider these difficulties and blueprints and to criticize them as freely as they may desire. I shall welcome any criticism, however destructive it may be to the ideas I set forth.
Let us define the terms I purpose using. First, repatriation:	To my mind repatriation
means bringing a man back to his home, either from overseas or from some other point in Canada, and putting him in the location from which he enlisted, or where he desires to be. That in itself constitutes a serious problem, and, as I shall presently show, one which is particularly serious for the R.C.A.F.
The next term is demobilization. Taken broadly I suppose that term would mean the dispersing of the armed forces into their civilian components or constituents. But actually it means more than that. It means more than the disbanding of the units. It involves personal demobilization; and that is paiticularly true in Canada, where, as I have often pointed out, our men before joining the forces were in civilian life, and in the vast majority of instances they will return to civilian life.
On top of this comes the problem of predemobilization education, which on a former occasion was explained to the house by my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). When we use that term we are referring to such education and training as we can give members of the armed forces while they are still under our jurisdiction, and before they are discharged into civilian life.
Finally comes rehabilitation, the problem of putting the former civilian who hhs served as a soldier back into a position where he may take his part in the civilian life of our country.
These are the problems with which we have to deal, and, following what was said by my colleague the Minister of National Defence, 1 propose immediately to state that the last named, rehabilitation, is not a matter which should be undertaken by the armed services or by the departments which look after the armed services. These are matters which have been discussed before. They were considered after the last war by various committees and by the house. I refer back to the pension committee of 1917. I have not the names of all the members who served on that committee, but among them were such men as Hon. Doctor Beland, Lord Bennett and Hon. Charles Marcil, outstanding men of that day, each of whom had to do with first framing the policy dealing with returning soldiers.

War Appropriation-Air Services
At that time there was conflict between what might be called the military or service mentality, and the civilian mentality. This conflict arose largely out of the question of the medical treatment of soldiers, but was found in some degree through the whole programme.
The report of the committee is too long to read in full, but if lion, members are interested in this phase of the matter I commend to their attention the report of the pension committee of 1917, at page 486 of volume XIII. There is the military point of view, but I believe in what I shall read will be found sufficient of the alternative or civilian proposals to permit the committee to understand what was being discussed. This is what we find:
In dealing with the question of the enlisted soldier, the end immediately in view must be borne in mind. All agencies brought to bear upon the citizen recruit have but one object, namely, ultimately to place a trained, disciplined fighting man on the firing line. It is therefore unquestionably admitted that the preparation of the soldier for active service should be in the hands of experienced military men.
When, however, the citizen soldier has become unfitted for further military service, or when the need no longer exists, it is desirable that he be returned to civil life with the least possible friction or delay. His goal now is a normal civil life, and all measures taken on his behalf should be with the purpose of making him once again a producer and a self-supporting citizen. It is, therefore, reasonable to assume that his restoration to civilian status is an undertaking likely to be best accomplished under civilian guidance. That is to say, as men df military experience are judged most capable of making soldiers out of civilians, so men of civil experience may rightly be regarded as best adapted for remaking civilians out of returned soldiers.
Then they go on to deal with the civilian point of view in respect of wounded and disabled men in connection with the following matters:
Hospital care and treatment.
Functional restoration and artificial limbs.
Vocational training and reeducation.
Casualties' pay and allowances in Canada.
Soldiers' homes.
Cooperation with provincial employment bureaux.
Any relief or disablement fund which may be found necessary.
And in respect of fit men:
Cooperation with the military authorities, with provincial governments and other agencies upon all matters affecting their return to civil life.
Supervision of voluntary organizations of and on behalf of returned soldiers.
That was the civilian point of view. The report continues:
Your committee, unable to reconcile these two divergent views in such a manner as to secure agreeent, is reluctantly compelled to leave the 
question of the control of the agencies for the care and treatment of returned soldiers without a recommendation on its part, having endeavoured in the previous paragraphs to state, with tairness to both contentions, the arguments in support of each view.
That report was made in July, and in February, 1918, the government set up the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment to do the specific things that were laid down here as the things to be presented from the civil side of the argument. After that, veterans' affairs and soldier problems were dealt with by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment.
It is easy for anyone to set out a theory and say that this can be done easily and rapidly. We hear the cliche that we should put our service machinery into reverse in order to solve our rehabilitation problems. It is easy to say, for instance, that one could take the recruiting officers, the men who went into industry to get the men to be put in the army, and use them to put the men back into industry. It may be said that we could use the recruiting offices with their selection boards and trade test boards for the purpose of selecting and trade testing men for a particular industry, and so on all down the line. This all looks well and I suppose it could be made the theme of an excellent speech. I realize that I may be subject to considerable criticism when I say that I do not think it will always work. It is quite possible that we may have to go beyond just simply putting our engines into reverse.
Then there is another cliche commonly used
that we should keep our men in the army until we find them jobs. I have no objection to that as a theory, but I fear that it will not work out in practice. For instance, I have been told that it would be a good idea to use the manning depot at Toronto, which is capable of taking care of from two to three thousand men. It is said' that this depot could be used for the accommodation of young men attending Toronto university. They would be kept under our control until such time as they had finished their courses. Again I realize there may be a difference of opinion, but I suggest that this might not work out. You would have two or three thousand boys still in the air force. If they are still in the air force they would retain their uniforms. They would be drilled in order to justify their use of the uniform. After morning drill they would go up to Toronto university. The lowest man in the military heirarchy, the LAC, might be first in the class in law and he would be taking orders from his wing commander, who might be just barely getting by with his examinations.

War Appropriation-Air Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: You think that there would be a lack of discipline?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is nothing especially unusual about that.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am simply quoting the
cliche that they should be kept in the army until jobs are found for them. As I say, in my opinion it would hardly work under those circumstances. If something else, is meant; if it is meant that we should continue to give them the same pay, the same financial advantages or otherwise, as they would receive if they remained in the service, then that would be another question. I submit that that is a matter which has to be dealt with by the civilian agency which deals with the man and not by the military service agency. The point I am trying to make is that the service agencies are not the proper departments to look after the man in civil life, except to make such preparations for his future career in civilian life as can be made while he remains in the service while the war is on, or while demobilization is on-which may be a long period; or while the period of occupying Europe is on, or while the period of policing Europe is on, or while we are still at war with Japan, which may be long after the end of the war with Germany.
Some of my officers think that I am pigheaded when I cannot agree with the theory that the service should look after these men up until the time when they are fully established in civilian life. My recollection of the last war is that there was an eagerness, almost amounting to mutiny, to get out of the units as quickly as possible. I admit that in this war the mentality is different. I fully recognize that men are younger, that many of them never had any other job. They realize there is some security in the armed services where they get three meals a day. There is perhaps a different mentality in the boys of to-day than there was in those of twenty-five years ago, but when the incentive to drill in order to fight, when the incentive to undergo discipline in order to be better fighters to beat the enemy is gone, when they remain under those conditions for four, five or six months after hostilities have ceased, there is a possibility they will be bored to death and will no longer want to remain in their units.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Will not a great deal depend upon the availability of jobs and other opportunities for these boys when they are ready to enter civilian life? If there are no opportunities available there would be an inducement for them to stay longer in the service. On the other hand, if there are
opportunities available in civilian life the boys will want to get the best ones as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I quite agree with my hon. friend. Whatever we have in the way of rehabilitation grants, in the way of service gratuities, or whatever we do in the way of finding them jobs, none of this will be any' good if our national economy does not progress to the point where there will be opportunities for these men to work and earn a decent living.
Having perhaps lightly laid aside the responsibilities of the service with regard to rehabilitation, properly so-called, and again subject to any opposite viewpoints which may be expressed, I come now to matters under our jurisdiction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Are you and the pensions department in agreement on these matters?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I have explained how the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment was set up to deal with the rehabilitation of the returned soldier. The service has a responsibility in connection with repatriation. The civilians cannot do that; they cannot bring back our men. The service has a responsibility in connection with demobilization, and also in connection with the priorities of demobilization, as to both units and individuals. My colleague, the Minister of National Defence, has spoken of our plans and the set-up which in fact is working now. There shall be in each department a director of demobilization who will be charged with all the duties connected with repatriation and demobilization. [DOT]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
That is in the three
services?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Each service; there shall be one in each service. He will correlate his activities with those of the other services through a demobilization council of the three services. Then, in order to get in closer touch with the civilian agencies-because after all the services must know what plans are being made by the civilian agencies-there will be an interdepartmental board composed of representatives of the three services, representatives of the Department of Pensions and National Health, who are charged with the rehabilitation; representatives of the Department of Labour, which is charged with the actual placements; and representatives of the department of reconstruction when it comes to be constructed.
Now, in order to show the importance which in common with my colleagues I attach to the

War Appropriation-Air Services
quality of the person who must head up this demobilization-and I say right away that I have not found him yet, although I have had my eye on two or three likely ones-I should like to quote a letter which I have sent to the air officer commanding-in-chief overseas, Air-Marshal Breadner:
I am looking for a man to head up a directorate of demobilization. He would not have a large staff. His job would be to coordinate all the work now going on along those lines in A.M.P. Division-
That is, the air member for personnel.
-and elsewhere. His duties would be something like this:	(a) to interview repatriated
personnel and try to fit them into our organization here;
That is to say, when men are about to be repatriated from overseas and they desire to stay in the air force, to try to find what kind of jobs we shall have for them here.
(b) to sit in with army and navy, with veterans' welfare department, Department of Labour, and with the new department of reconstruction; (c) he would do some organizing overseas; (d) to start pre-demobilization education, and he might be your representative on the new joint demobilization committee; (e) he would be charged with the explanation of rehabilitation proposals to R.C.A.F. personnel -overseas and in Canada; (f) he would probably have to shuttle back and forth between here and the Lhnted Kingdom.
His qualifications must be high. He must be an overseas man with actual fighting experience. He must have the imagination, organizing ability and possibly business experience. He must talk the overseas boys' language.
This superman should be fairly high up, a wing commander or group captain, but if he measures up he deserves promotion anyway and he will get it. Give me the names of your recommendations.
I have had two or three recommendations. Unfortunately these lads who are recommended-I have had two or three in mind- .almost invariably get a better job before I can lay my hands on them in actual operations, .and they will not come back. One of them is now high up, connected with the tactical -air*force; another one was heading a squadron in England and has done marvellous work; he is now in charge of a wing in the proposed invasion. I am going to get a man sooner or later, but I do not want to take anybody to fill the job unless it is possible to get the very best.
This letter explains, as much as a speech would, just the type of man required, and I think the committee will agree with me that this is the type of man we want. It is proposed that he shall be directly under the minister and talk to the minister direct on all these matters. It is a matter of such importance that it becomes the minister's duty and responsibility to look after it himself.

In connection with that, there has been developed in the R.C.A.F., and to some extent in the army, plans for personnel counselling. I do not like the term; "personnel counselling" does not look like the kind of term I want to use, but I cannot find a better one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And it does not sound like your language, either.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Well, if I wanted to use high-flown language I could probably call him a "career consultant" or something of the kind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is still less like you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Better get a medical man for that job.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The intention-and we have a plan which is actually in operation-is to help R.C.A.F. men and women to help themselves. Our men and women are not the type who wish to become dependent on any paternalism; they want to stand on their own feet. The R.C.A.F. intends to provide them with information, advice and direction, so that they may be as self-reliant after the war as they have proved themselves to be in combat. We wish to sustain their confidence in us by letting them know that we are interested in them personally and intend to give them every assistance to make good on their own.
The plan is one of consultation and advice. In consultation with every man and woman in the air force, wherever located, advisers will provide facts upon which a career may be planned. Facts will be available on the interests, aptitudes and experience of the person, on the occupations for which he or she is suited, on the opportunities in those occupations, and on the assistance which can be provided right now for making progress toward a chosen objective.. This is not job placement; it is career planning, so that those who take advantage of it may have something of value to offer, instead of being dependent on someone to give them a job.
Many of our airmen have endured the strains and hazards of a long tour of combat. Nothing will help them more to free themselves from the travail of war than a goal toward which they can plan and work. This goal we intend to provide.
The results of the R.C.A.F. plan of personnel selection have been reinterpreted in terms of civil occupations. This enables us to indicate to a man just where he stands, having regard to his ability, aptitudes and training, in relation to men already employed in various professions, occupations and trades. Thus in

War Appropriation-Air Services
choosing a career he can judge for himself the type of competition he will meet in various vocations.
Many employers have already been contacted, and representative professional, business and industrial groups have been consulted concerning the practical applications of the plan.
One group of consultants have already completed their training. These men and women have all had extensive service in the R.C.A.F., and were selected as having the necessary personal qualifications for this work. They are the vanguard of a larger group of officers who will spread out to R.C.A.F. units, both here and overseas, to aid men and women plan careers.
Educational and technical courses will be provided to suit the career plans. Thus any man or woman can utilize any available time in purposeful activity in keeping with his or her career plan. Many such courses are available; others will be added.
A record of consultation will be provided for each person which will give details concerning the planned career, as well as any progress the person makes while in the service.
Since this deals entirely with the personnel who are still in the service, it falls within the scope of R.C.A.F. responsibility. It is concerned with the welfare of personnel prior to their release to civil life, and hence does not encroach upon the activity of those government departments responsible for rehabilitation and occupational placement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Are the same privileges and opportunities to apply in equal measure to the army and the navy?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Oh, yes; I am quite sure they are. We hope that this service will enable R.C.A.F. personnel to take -full advantage of the provisions already made for the purposes of demobilization and rehabilitation.
This looks like a good blueprint. I am not going to guarantee that it will always work. I am putting it forth as a plan and as a blueprint. It should work, if we can get the proper men to do the counselling or the advising or the consulting. But everything along these lines is dependent on the human factor. We might set to work now and during the demobilization period to train a boy to be a lawyer or a doctor. He falls in love with some girl, gets married and decides that he would rather live on his wife's relatives. Where are we then? We have wasted all our time and our money. But it is an attempt to assure these boys that at least we are goirig to try to do something for them.
All this is connected with pre-demobilization training. I am really putting the cart before ' the horse. Repatriation comes first, and in repatriation we have, as I think the committee will readily understand, a very special problem in the R.C.A.F.
First, it is in the character of our boys- which also applies to demobilization. They are young; a great many of them have never had any jobs; they have no real conception of what the struggle of life may be except from what they have learned in their homes; they have no real conception, from personal contacts, of the difficulties of making a living. Repatriation is our difficult point. As I have explained to, the house on many occasions, many more of our boys are in R.A.F. squadrons than are in R.C.A.F. squadrons. We have to get our hands on them before we even think of bringing them home, and that is not so easy, particularly in the midst of operations. We must not interfere with the fellow on operations in order to get our hands on him so as to get him ready to come back to Canada when demobilization comes. We must to a certain extent make plans, though certain plans can be made which will be immediately helpful.
In correspondence with Sir Archibald Sinclair, the Secretary of State for Air in the United Kingdom, and in recent discussions with Captain Balfour, I have come to an agreement on the matter and. as I advised the house some time ago, as will be seen in Hansard, a joint committee of the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F. has been set up. I did not advise [DOT] the house at that time, however, of the terms of reference proposed by Canada, which have not yet been accepted, though I have reason to believe they will be. The terms are these:
(a)	What methods and procedure should be followed in order to enable the Canadian government to proceed as rapidly and as efficiently as possible with R.C.A.F. repatriation and demobilization?
(b)	What steps can be taken now, and generally during the period, which shall precede the termination of the war against Germany, to bring about a regrouping of R.C.A.F. personnel, so that Canadian demobilization priorities may be made effective at the earliest possible date without injury to the common war effort?
(c)	What methods of procedure are to be followed so that R.C.A.F. personnel serving in R.A.F. units may have equal opportunity with R.C.A.F. personnel who are serving in Canada or in the R.C.A.F. personnel overseas, to take advantage of the Canadian government's plans for repatriation, demobilization and rehabilitation?

War Appropriation-Air Services
(d)	What methods and procedure should be followed in order to give R.C.A.F. personnel attached to the R.A.F. the benefits of pre-demobilization training and instruction to fit such personnel for civil life in Canada while still attached to the R.A.F.?
We added:
. The committee in their deliberation will be guided by the following principles:
(a)	That there shall be no interference with the most effective prosecution of the war.
(b)	That the highest consideration be given to ensuring to individual officers and airmen every possible opportunity for a successful postwar career.
(c)	That the process of demobilization shall be such as will assist to the greatest extent possible the effective recovery of the domestic economy of each country.
In connection with that, a reciprocal arrangement was entered into with the R.A.F., whereby our boys attached to the R.A.F. would take advantage of such pre-demobilization training as the R.A.F. is giving, and we on the other hand would give their boys attached to the R.C.A.F. such pre-demobilization training and education as we give to our boys.
I can see that this may not always be appropriate or useful. For example, I can hardly conceive that the training in agricultural pursuits given to men intending to settle in Kent or Devonshire, say, would be useful to a Canadian who intends to settle on the prairies or the bushlands of Ontario. Such training would not be of much use to him in the career he expects to undertake in the _ wilder parts of Canada. However, the will is there, the agreement is there, and something is sure to be got out of it.
Having dealt as far as I can with repatriation, in order to give the committee some idea of the difficulties that confront us, let me deal with what really belongs to repatriation, the question of priorities on demobilization. That again should be divided into two parts, priorities by units or groups and priorities by individuals. Priorities by units would apply more readily to the army than to the air force. It is easy enough to say that the first division shall come back first, the second divisoin second, and so forth; but in the air force it is very much more difficult, since the men are so widely scattered, These matters have been and are being discussed, and1 on certain questions no definite decision has been reached.
On the question of priority there appeared to be two distinct problems: Should priority of discharge be given overseas personnel, and should a system of individual priorities be set

up to apply to the service as a whole, with the locus of the individual concerned being only one factor out Of many?
In considering the first of these questions, it is felt that priority of discharge should be given men serving overseas, but in view of the obstacles in the way of such a plan it is not always possible or feasible. The factors involved have been carefully reviewed and a number of them have been set out hereunder for consideration. I may say that this is a report of some of my officers on the subject. It is not a precedent, and I do not want it to create a precedent, whereby reports of officers are made public. But this is a matter in which the public is very widely interested. The public should be interested in the discussion as between different schools of thought before hard and fast rules are made of them, which will be so binding that it will be very difficult to retrace our steps. It is for that reason that I take the committee into my confidence and ask hon. members not to use this as a precedent against me if I say that I cannot produce a document inasmuch as it is a document from an officer of the department to the minister, made in confidence.
The reasons for priority of demobilization for personnel serving overseas are:
(a)	Publio opinion will undoubtedly clamour for preferential treatment for personnel serving overseas.
(b)	Such personnel deserve priority on demobilization and in any plans for reestablishment which may be undertaken by the government or by industry.
(c)	Since they have been separated from their families and generally have been unable to return on leave, they should be given the earliest possible opportunity of reunion.
(d>) Since their' lives and those of their families have been disturbed to a greater degree than is the case with personnel who serve in Canada only, it seems only fair that they be given the opportunity of returning to a normal civilian state. Pending the reorganization of the permanent forces after the war, certain installations and equipment in Canadh must be manned and maintained by service personnel. This will have to be done in the first instance by personnel now discharged, but the troops overseas should be given the first opportunity of doing that work.
I come now to the reasons for demobilization of personnel as soon as available, which is the contrary view:
(a)	Public opinion would be strongly against retaining longer than necessary men conscripted in Canada who have volunteered for overseas service.

War Appropriation-Air Services
(b)	Personnel in excess of requirements would result in the following additional expense to the country:
Pay and allowances; gratuities or rehabilitation benefits which would increase with the length of service; amounts necessary for subsistence; medical care, et cetera; retention of buildings which should be released for civilian use.
The difficulty of maintaining the morale and discipline of these services in Canada is another matter to be considered. That would have to be considered if they had to wait demobilization of those serving overseas. And' then man-power will be needed for civilian industry and there will be pressure from civilian industry to get at the nearest source of man-power. On the other hand it would be difficult to repatriate the personnel from overseas because it may be difficult to get transport. There would be the problem of shifting personnel from one theatre of war to another when we go toward the Japanese theatre and so on: It may cause innumerable difficulties in the supply of shipping. That is the general system. ' No matter what we do, we must aim at seeing to it that the man from overseas gets preferential treatment in demobilization and in repatriation, but always bearing in mind the fact that there may be difficulties in carrying out that principle as we' have laid it down.
Then, with regard to individual priorities, there is a great difference of opinion. However, I believe two principles can be accepted by all. (a) No individual should be demobilized so long as his retention is essential to service requirements, (b) Personnel desiring delayed demobilization may be retained provided they can be usefully employed and fulfil certain conditions laid down. In connection with that there is, as hon. members know, the point system. The point system was elaborated by the central committee on post-war reconstruction set up by the Conservative and Unionist party in Great Britain in a pamphlet called 'booking Ahead". So far as I know, this point system has not as yet been definitely accepted by the armed services overseas; in fact there is a great deal of opposition to it. I shall quote from it:
In their search for a solution to the many problems which arise from the definition of priorities, the committee has under review a scheme of "points" which is strongly recommended for favourable consideration.
The scheme attaches a specified value to the presence or absence of certain factors influencing the individual case for demobilization. As an example of the working of the scheme, let us suppose it is decided that fifteen per cent of the personnel of a certain unit can be demobilized. The records offices, which would be
given details not normally in their possession, would forward the names of those who had the highest "score" on some such basis as the following-
And here come the points:
-so many points for service on or before certain dates, service overseas, steps of promotion, age group, marriage, number of children, employment immediately available, one-man business, demand for personnel in trade or profession, and interruption of education, with a subtraction of points for desirability of the man's retention in the services.
To operate such a scheme there would have to be close liaison-
Then they go on to show where cooperation takes place. We have had a look at that in an endeavour to apply it to conditions here. Some of the officers have worked out a point system for the R.C.A.F., taking into consideration not all the points mentioned here, but such points as length of service, nature of service and dependent children. I may be boring the committee with all this, but somebody is going to put it on Hansard and it may as well be put there by me. I want the committee to know I am not laying this down as the law of the Medes and Persians. I am saying that these are plans which have been submitted in other parts of the world and are being considered by various departments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The committee will pay a great deal of attention to what the minister says.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I hope to get a lot of advice from the committee. It is recommended that value be given to the different factors as follows. We are taking only four of these factors: (a) length of service, one unit for each month of service; (b) age, one unit for each year of age; (c) nature of service (combat service), 25 units; (d) dependent children, five units for first child; ten units for more than one child. Attached is a table. I should like to lay it on the table.
Perhaps the committee will follow the details of one case. Let us take a married man, thirty-five years old, with two dependent children and two-year service. His score would be thirty-five for age, two-year service, one unit for each month, twenty-four; two children, ten units for more than one child, a total of sixty-nine. That is the priority score. Let us take a man thirty-five years old with two dependent children, two years overseas and combat service. You would add twenty-five points for combat service, and his score would be ninety-four. Let us take another example, a married man forty years old with three years' service and no dependent children. He would

War Appropriation-Air Services
have a score of forty for his age, plus thirty-six for his three-year service, giving him a total score of seventy-six. If the same man had combat service his score would be seventy-six plus twenty-five, or a total of a hundred and one. The scores have been worked out in a number of cases, and if the committee will permit me I shall table it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I thought the minister gave some points to a man who had a one-man business.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is not the Conservative plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: You are not considering that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: My officers have worked it out only on the basis of four different factors. We might work it out on any number of factors. I brought this with me to show the committee how it. would work. If the committee will permit me I shall give the views of the opponents of the point scheme.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: How long is the term of enlistment in the air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: No term.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: They are in until they are discharged?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Not like the last war?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
No.
There is some opposition which merits serious consideration before we embark on such a plan. The point system is considered unsatisfactory, (1) because it is complicated. Definitions are required for the factors involved. If we mention the factors involved in the Unionist system it will get more and more involved and more and more complicated. We shall need a lot of chartered accountants to add up the score before we get through.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We are short of them now.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
We are short of them now. (2) It is not altogether fair; 725,000 individuals could not be put into about a hundred priority groups without injustice being felt by a very great number. And in my opinion here is where it fails, unless we can find something to improve it. In the middle brackets many thousands of personnel would have about the same points, particularly if you tak* a large number of matters on which you can obtain a score. If you gave the long term people a sufficient number of points they would have an easy lead. You would
fMr Power.]
get a number who would have about the same number of points and then the fighting would begin all over again as between the people in the middle brackets, but there is no provision for priorities among men with the same score. They would have to have pull with Laurier. (3) It discriminates against the veterans' guard and older soldiers, for whom accelerated demobilization would be harmful, in the main, because of special difficulties in rehabilitation, and against the jmunger personnel who have never had civilian employment, or who should complete his schooling without further delay. (4) It reduces speed in discharge, especially if discharge is to be delayed on account of vocational training and other rehabilitation measures. It is felt that the prime factor in demobilization is the successful employment of ex-service personnel. There would be a public outcry against keeping personnel in the services on pay and allowances if by earlier discharge they could get a job and become reestablished.
My own opinion is both points of view should be carefully examined, and I should like to hear from anyone who has any views on the subject. We know what we want to do, namely, to bring those who can be brought home as soon as possible after the hostilities are over. Then give them all the predemobilization training we can, in the most useful way, so as to do the individual the greatest amount of good in his future career. We have plans and blueprints to accomplish this, but, as I said, I will not guarantee that they will all be successful. We must be prepared-and I think this is something to which we should give the utmost consideration- for the immediate let-down, moral and mental, which will attack these boys. They will have been three or four years trained, taught and groomed to one objective, one purpose; and that purpose and objective will be gone. The enemy will have been defeated; they will have completely lost their orientation. Many of them never will have had any other orientation than fighting. An organized body of men solidly knit together to act for one common purpose in this war will, unless we are very careful, suddenly become a mob of individuals each seeking his own objective, if indeed he has any at the moment.
I do not want to be an alarmist, but with the history of developments after the last war imprinted in my mind I fear that we might have mutinies such as we had then. I fear the development of a state of mind which might colour and distort their whole future outlook, and we must try to develop

War Appropriation-Air Services
some new objective for them. As I said, if we discipline a body of men with a common purpose and objective, to defeat the enemy; then if we go to them and say that each individual will get so much in the way of dollars or so much in the way of treatment; if we develop their purely selfish instincts, the purely materialistic side, then we shall have a panic to see who will get first what is required, and the devil take the hindmost. In other words we cannot and should not promise each individual that everything he desires will be handed to him on a silver platter. Let there be a new order. It matters not what the new order is. It may be the new order of my hon. friends, on a socialistic pattern; it may be a new order on a free enterprise pattern; it may be a new order on the pattern of New Democracy or Social Credit, or it may be a combination of all three.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Don't forget your own Bloc Populaire.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
It may be on the order of the Bloc Populaire. I have no objection to the returning soldier becoming an adherent of any political creed; on the contrary I hope he will, for I want him to be thinking of the future of Canada. I want him to be thinking of the future along the lines of any one of the political.parties represented in this house; for as long as he is thinking of the future of Canada he is doing what I think he should be doing rather than thinking of his own selfish and material interests. It is Canada he has to be working for when he comes back.
It is for this reason that, while I do not disagree with all this work in connection with demobilization and placing a value on each man's services, I think it has little to do with questions of repatriation, rehabilitation and so on. After all I am cynic enough, having been in the house for all these years, to know that he will pretty well get what he wants anyway, out of one political party or the other. If we teach him that he can only get what he "wants by agitation, by thinking of himself and of his own interests, then we make a bad citizen of him.
I should like to try out on this committee some views on this subject which I have tried out elsewhere already, without any response whatever. We should explain to our men that the winning of the war was not the end of all things. I fear that after the last war most of us felt that this was the end, that this was what we had been struggling toward for three years, and that now the job was done. Let us tell our boys that the winning of the war was only the means to assure us and the world
the right to continue unhampered and unimpeded in our peaceful pursuits, that it was only a means to an end, not the end itself. What is the greatest, the most pressing and most important pursuit we can have, if it is not to make our own country great; great in industry, great in agriculture, great in commerce, great in development, and great as a nation? During the course of the last war we were promised material things: "A land fit for heroes to live in," and "On your return Canada will be yours." I fear that we paid too much attention to those material things that were being promised to us and did not pay enough attention to the spiritual side of trying to become a good citizen, and I say that without casting any reflection at all upon those who returned from the last war.
Our boys must be given a new target, some task to look forward to, to soften the impact of the inevitable let-down; and that target must be attacked with all the ambition and all the patriotic fervour of their wartime activity. A great man promised victory in the war through blood, sweat and tears, and we can set another task; the making of Canada, through labour and perseverance and energy. Let the brawn and the brain and the courage of these thousands of young men be turned to the development of their own country, and no nation on God's green earth can equal us. Let us emphasize the spiritual side of the peace-time task at least as much as the material side. When these boys return to Canada this country will be theirs, but theirs to mould, to develop, to build and to make capable of fulfilling its great destiny as a nation. The true glamour of peace must be made to replace the transient glamour of war. We have told our boys what a noble and heroic thing it was to apply themselves to the science of war. Let us tell them what a noble thing it is to apply themselves to the arts of peace. We have taught them how to destroy; let us teach them how to build. They went forth to defend Canada; let them go forth to develop Canada. Let our boys understand that when the last gun has been fired and the last bomb dropped, their task will have only begun. Duties and responsibilities as heavy as those they now bear await them on their return; duties and responsibilities, and opportunities too, if we make them for them, limited only by the great extent of their country and by its vast potential resources, industrial, natural and commercial. They will have conquered a hard, bitter human enemy; they can and will conquer natural obstacles. Let them subjugate the land, exploit the waters and control the air of this country. They will not only have won a livelihood;

War Appropriation-Air Services
they will have served their country truly and well. Let them not believe for one instant that the end of the war is the end of all things for them. The great adventure of fighting, the hazard of dying for their country will be over, but the greatest adventure, the strenuous one of living for their country, will be only beginning.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The truly excellent statement given by the minister last Tuesday and to-day should fill every member of this house and every Canadian with great pride. The minister mentioned "the effort of the Canadian people as a whole". The success of the air force in all its branches, right from the dull job of the radio mechanic through to that of the bomber pilot, has been due in part to the great spirit of the Canadian people, who know no bounds when they are aroused, and in part to the fact that as far as the air force goes we have yet to see the hand of politics. Unlike the army, an air force officer will seldom if ever tell you his politics. It is difficult to talk very long to an army officer before the subject of politics is discussed.
The staggering information the minister placed on record Tuesday night, showing that the Canadian air effort represented between twenty-two per cent and twenty-five per cent of the aircrew or of the total air effort of the joint British tactical air effort-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The hon. member should stick to his first expression-aircrew.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes, aircrew-is, I say, remarkable.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is in Europe.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Yes, that is in Europe. But it shows something more; it shows that Canada, with only 12,000,000 people, can produce in a short period of time an air force the equal of, if not superior to that of any other nation. The fact that our squadrons are used extensively on the very difficult job of pathfinding for the bomber squadrons, one requiring the highest degree of skill, shows the degree of technical excellence attained by Canadian aircrew.
The diversification of our air effort was emphasized by the minister. He referred to the radio mechanics, the personnel manning radio location stations, for the bomber command and the fighter command, the Atlantic patrol, the coastal command, the Atlantic air bases for the protection of our own sovereign air, and the bases for the protection of our Pacific coast. The vast variety in numbers and descriptions of our air effort has only begun to be appre-

dated, and I am glad- that for the country's sake the minister has placed the statistics on record.
Our air effort imposes upon Canada a great responsibility, greater than many of us realize. It imposes, too, the responsibility of maintaining ourselves as a great peace-time air power. As the minister pointed out in his speech, as reported at page 1029 of Hansard, a post-war civil aviation committee has been set up. I shall not read the paragraph, but hon. members will find it at the point I have indicated.	'
Our air effort is a combined one. While we have forty-four squadrons of our own, yet the bulk of our effort is that'which is combined with those of the British, Australian, and the other united nations who are operating against the common, enemy. After the war is over, we cannot allow this effort to revert to a purely Canadian one. We shall have our responsibilities to help keep the air lanes of the world free and open. We have probably become, or shall be by the time the war is over, the third largest air power in the world. In point of geography we are located centrally, so far as future civil aviation is concerned. Yet we have attained our position only in conjunction and cooperation with the United' Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and the other nations of the commonwealth. Had we tried to run the show on our own, we might have met with some success, it would have been greatly reduced.
Our immediate responsibility is to see to it that, from the civilian point of view, our postwar air effort is mapped out in conjunction with the other nations of the commonwealth. We cannot afford not to cooperate with the United Kingdom to the fullest degree in peace time, as we are now doing in war time. If we fail to give this cooperation we shall be relegated to a place not third greatest among the air powers of the world, but to one comparable with our population, and standing away down the list of the world powers. Therefore our first responsibility, in the light of our great air effort in the war, is as I have stated.
The minister mentioned the ratio of casualties to decorations. It is interesting to note that one decoration has been received for every ten casualties inflicted. To my mind this more than anything else shows the efficiency and striking power of our air force. I believe it is much greater than we had expected. Let us remember that every bomber destroyed has carried a crew of from five to ten men, and sometimes more. Accordingly for every large bomber shot down we may say that one decoration has been given. Surely

War Appropriation-Air Services
this is some indication of the teamwork and heroism of the young men who are dtoing this magnificent job.
I do not believe the committee realizes the magnitude of a single raid against Germany. I shall not speak about groundcrew, but would confine what I have to say to the aircrew organization necessary for a thousand-bomber raid. The number employed equals approximately the number of a division of infantry. Within the space of a few hours that division must be taken into the air, flown 600 miles to within two vertical miles, probably less, of the target, and flown back to the home bases. The staggering cost and the amazing teamwork which goes into that effort cannot be emphasized too greatly.
I should like to make a suggestion to the minister in connection with what he said this afternoon. Up to now our air effort can be considered our major one. Hon. members will be called upon to look after and to provide for the future lives of all those young airmen who each night are risking their lives over Germany. Yet, with I believe one exception, hon. members have not had the actual experience which would give them an understanding of the problems involved. Newspaper men have been given this opportunity. I suggest that certain members be allowed to make an operational flight. We shall be called upon to look after these men when they come back and I think we might have some first-hand experience of the problems they meet daily.
The minister went on to discuss repatriation, demobilization and rehabilitation. He mentioned the difficulties of repatriation and they are probably greater than he intimated. We have members of the air force, such as radio mechanics, who have been located for years in 'distant outposts. These men being in isolated positions have had little opportunity of advancement and they have seen little service apart from their work as technicians. In many instances they are, to use the current expression, "browned off." These men should be among the first to be repatriated because their problem is an extremely difficult one. As the minister has pointed out, we have men in the -operational groups of Royal Air Force. Some of the men, particularly those in the far east, may have to remain in the service for years before they are repatriated.
I agree entirely with what the minister said with regard to the problem of demobilization. There is nothing worse than to keep a soldier in the army with nothing to do after the actual fighting is over. His life becomes useless routine. Every parade, every fatigue,
or every duty that he must undertake becomes an added irritation. Eventually morale decreases and rioting breaks out. I saw some of the rioting that took place in England after the last war because I was in a camp that actually did riot.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Shame!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I expect that the hon. member for Fraser Valley was also in a camp that rioted. It is easy to be carried away by the desire to destroy things, particularly when one has nothing to do. There is the old saying that the devil finds work for idle hands, and that is particularly true in demobilization centres. Demobilization must take place as soon as possible.
There is one psychological angle I-think the minister has overlooked. When this war is over, these men must be able to go into useful work. We must get over any idea that the work provided for -the veterans of this war is to be provided in a spirit of gratitude.* That is the wrong premise to adopt. The work they are to be called upon to do must be work that is useful and essential. If that is not done the same psychology will apply. The men will regard their work as something that has no value. This would prove to be one of the greatest causes of the destruction of the spirit of our service men and it must not happen. There are one or two matters I should like to take up with the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) when his bills are before him, but now 1 only want to emphasize that the work provided for these men must be useful and essential. That factor must take precedence over all others.
The young men of this war have been trained to take instant action to destroy. That has been their whole fighting training-to destroy the enemy. The question of cost or wastage of material never enters into the problem at all; it is simply a question of kill or be killed.' The opposite rule applies to civilian and commercial life. No matter under what system we operate, cost governs the operation. Our difficulty will be much greater after this war because the personnel are more highly trained. The young man who has been flying a Lancaster bomber with 5,000 horse-power and with his bomb bays filled with weapons capable of creating acres of destruction will not be particularly interested in a repetitive job on an assembly line, or in, shall we say, selling soap retail or any other similar commodity. He will want a job where he can utilize his intellect and it is going to be extremely difficult to provide that job. I think

War Appropriation-Air Services
the minister was right in bringing up this question this afternoon. If we make promises to the people in the forces to-day and do not carry out those promises we are certainly taking the first step toward revolution.
The minister did not deal with one question, the size of the postwar air force. Naturally he cannot give any specific details, but I think some statement should be made to indicate that an opportunity will be provided for some of the men in the force to maintain themselves in the Royal Canadian Air Force after the war. There should be some statement that after the war we shall not again abandon the arts of war. That statement should be made now. I know it is axiomatic that we shall not do away with the air force, but it must be remembered that after the last war we abolished most of our naval, military and air force establishments. We abolished the Royal Naval College; we very nearly abolished the Royal Military College. There swept over the country a wave of pacificism which laid the seeds of our lack of preparation when this war began.
In conclusion, the minister mentioned what might be called the pragmatic philosophy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: What is that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Merely this, that the individual looks after himself and is not interested in the welfare of the state. A purely selfish outlook was preached and practised after the end of the last war, and it led us into the greatest possible amount of difficulty. The old army saying, "So-and-so you, George, I'm all right," became almost the national spirit. We must be careful to avoid similar disillusionment after this war is over; because if at the end of this war we are at the opening of a better era of peace and good order among all nations, yet because we have preached the philosophy of selfishness our men will come out looking for something to get rather than something to serve, and we shall enter into another cycle which may go down into another war, a new depression and chaos even worse than the two we have already seen.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the estimates of the Department of National Defence for Air, I wish first to touch on the propriety of a member in uniform speaking on estimates of the department in which he serves.
In the British House of Commons the sharpest criticism and the most helpful suggestions on service matters have come from those who are in uniform. Members of parliament, of course, are expected to speak on subjects of which they have extensive knowledge; and who in this parliament have better

opportunities of acquiring extensive knowledge of the services than those in uniform? In this country, however, there seems to be a desire to restrain or, as I believe the legal word is, to proscribe a member of parliament in uniform from speaking on service matters in this chamber. Actually the very delicate position of a member of parliament in uniform is covered by P.C. 3205, which in the air force becomes air force general order No. 21. The hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for Weyburn, and the hon. member for York-Sunbury at the last sitting of the house discussed to some extent this order as it affects men who hope to be candidates in the next election. I would say that in this respect this order is more generous than the corresponding British order. It is rather with the effect of this order on a member of parliament that I am concerned. Provision is made for adequate and, indeed, very generous leave to attend parliament, provided^ of course, the exigencies of the service permit. If the man is in uniform his first responsibility still must be to the service; otherwise he should resign his commission and return to parliament, if he finds that he has to put parliament ahead of his service when he is in the service. However, a member of parliament who is given this leave is subject to the following restriction, that a person granted leave for this purpose shall not disclose any information of a service nature which he has acquired in the course of his duties as a member of the armed forces. Well, quite frankly I will tell the committee that everything I know about the air force I have learned during the course of my duties in the air force. Quite frankly also I will say that as a member of parliament I do not intend to be restrained or proscribed by anyone outside the walls of this chamber. Therefore, despite this air force general order No. 21, I now propose to discuss the Department of National Defence for Air on the basis of things which I have learned while in the service.
I do not propose to speak on any operational matter in the service. After all, I am a very junior officer and am not qualified to discuss the purpose and the value of strategy which has been planned by the leaders of the service. I know that in this respect I am very much different from the hon. member for Weyburn. I got Hansard all the time I was overseas. Last year's Hansard I got in Sicily. I read it with interest because I was a member. The members of my squadron read it because there was nothing else to read. All of us, however, read with both,

War Appropriation-Air Services
I may say, amazement and amusement the fact that the hon. member for Weyburn criticized the Dieppe operation on the geographical knowledge which he had acquired in a one-day Cook's tour of Dieppe in 1936 and the military knowledge he had acquired through an honorary chaplain's commission in the militia in peace time. Everyone in the squadron I was with had waded ashore in the invasion of Sicily. None of us felt prepared to discuss even the invasion of Sicily with that operational background, so that the committee will understand what I mean when I say that we were amused and amazed.
I propose, however, to discuss certain of the administrative policies of the Royal Canadian Air Force, because that force is simply another branch of government as far as administration is concerned, and a member of parliament who can criticize, for example, the Department of Labour, as I have done, can criticize or praise the administration of the Royal Canadian Air Force or any other branch of the service.
First of all, I should like to commend the minister. I think I can truthfully say that the minister is the favourite minister of this house, because we know that he has been the driving power behind Canada's greatest single contribution to this war, the joint air training scheme. It is not only for his interest and activity in the operation of the R.C.A.F. that I commend him, but for the very intense personal interest which he takes in the welfare of every single man in the R.C.A.F. I cannot give a better example of that than the speech he has just made on the demobilization and rehabilitation of the men of his service.
The war is of course far from won, but planning ahead to give these young men in the R.C.A.F. some feeling of confidence in what is going to happen to them when the war does end is a very fine thing and most encouraging.
Since my return I have raised a number of 'ssues with the minister and have not always met with success, naturally, but have always met with every consideration.
A week ago in this house I asked a question about the retirement of quite a number of very senior air officers. The minister made a forthright reply, in which he said that the retirement was in no way a slur on any of these officers, but merely to remove what he called a "bottle-neck" or ceiling on promotion for those who had fought in this war and, to use his own words, "who should shortly assume command if the air force is to be the young and virile force which Canada wishes it to be." I am quite sure we all agree with that sentiment. Most of these senior leaders of the air force, however, are veterans of the last war, with distinguished records, who belong to what 100-68
is called the permanent force. The air force is their career. There are also senior officers who belong not to the permanent force but to the auxiliary force, which is the air force militia in peace time, and to the special reserve, citizen soldiers, as most of the air force are. I feel that if retirements are in order these men should be the first to be retired. They should be retired before those in the permanent force, and I say that for two reasons. The permanent force men have no civilian jobs to which they can go. The air force has been their career, whereas the special reserve senior officers must have left very good jobs to qualify for such a high rank at the beginning of the war.
The second reason is a monetary one. When you retire senior air force officers you retire them at a substantial pension, whereas the auxiliary officers go back to civilian life and civilian jobs, without pensions but with a generous gratuity, in their case, of one month's pay.
There is another point about retirements. Just under the ceiling of senior air officers who fought in the last war and have given wonderful leadership to the air force in this war is a layer of officers who were too young for the last war and whose rank was too high to justify sending them overseas in this war. In the rapidly expanding air force their ability and administrative training were of great use in this country. It will be a pity if the retirement of the veterans of the last war results in these men coming to the top. Tens of thousands of aircrew fighting overseas want to be led by men with real operational experience, if not experience in the last war, then experience gained in this one. To my knowledge, there is not an R.C.A.F. airman who has done a tour of operations overseas in this war who has yet achieved a rank higher than group captain. Generally we think of the air force as a keen, young, progressive service and the army is sometimes regarded as Tory-I withdraw that word; I will say as the slower or more reactionary of the services. However, I read with tremendous pride the statement by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) on the recent appointment of men leading combatant soldiers overseas, and I wish to put this list on the record:

That is one of the finest tributes that can be paid to the army, to say that they are led



War Appropriation-Air Services
by men who are making it a "young, virile and dynamic force". I served with the desert air force for about a year, and I believe, as most people overseas believe, that it is the most efficient fighting force in this war. No little part of its success is due to the leadership of Air Vice-Marshal Broadhurst, D.S.O., D.F.C., aged thirty-seven, who has done two full operational tours in this war. Not only has he directed the air force from the control room, but he has led them in battle. He was the first pilot to land in Sicily and the first pilot to land in Italy.
With this in mind I again urge that when those veterans with distinguished records in the last war are retired they be succeeded by men who have done at least one operational tour in this war.
Unlike the army, the air force is an entirely voluntary service. Unlike the army, we do not have a horrid word bandied around in the house but never appearing in Hansard. Every man who joined the air force joined for the duration, to serve wherever the country's enemies are to be found. Every one of them when he enlisted thought he would get overseas and many are disappointed, because of the enormous training establishment which we had set up in the country to bring into fruition the empire air training plan. The minister has announced that the plan is pretty well stabilized, and I should think there is a better chance to get many of these men overseas. Those who have been overseas for a long time would also have a better opportunity to return home.
I commend the minister for the fact that he has kept the Canada badge of the airmen as a symbol of overseas service. Most airmen are prouder to wear "Canada" on their shoulders than the service decoration on their chest, and I hope that at the end of the war every man in the air force will be carrying the name of his country on his shoulder.
May I speak shortly on behalf of Canadians in the Royal Air Force. The minister explained the other night what their status was. These are Canadians who could not get into the R.C.A.F. in peace time because we were so small, and hon. members to the left were obstructing the present Minister of Pensions and National Health when he was trying to expand the war services. These men could not get in just after the war began because our rapidly expanding service set a very high standard. These are the men who went to England on cattle-boats, working their way there in order to join the R.A.F. No single group of Canadians in this war have so gallant a record. Whereas most of the R.C-A.F. did

not start fighting in Europe until 1941, these men started on September 4, 1939, and they have fought in every battle in which the R.A.F. has been engaged-in France, Norway, Britain, Malta, the middle east and the far east. They have paid a very heavy price in casualties and have won great honour for our country.
The minister pointed out that Canada had no connection with them as far as finances are concerned. He went farther and stated that we were not identified with them in any other way. I think we are identified in another way. The early Canadian squadrons overseas were led by these Canadians in the R.A.F., because we did not possess men with that training at that time. The minister two years ago put on record the names of twenty-one men leading the Canadian squadrons. To my knowledge, ten of those twenty-one were Canadians in the R.A.F. I would remind him that his own son in Italy, serves in a Canadian squadron until recently led by one of the most gallant and dauntless of Canadians in the R.A.F., Wing Commander Stan Turner, D.F.C. and bar, of Toronto.
Very distinguished service has also been given to the R.C.A.F. by their present chief of air staff who for a long time served the R.C.A.F. as a Canadian in the R.A.F.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: May I add to what my hon. friend has said. The first squadron that fought as a Canadian squadron, 406 squadron, was composed entirely of Canadians in the R.A.F. and it was called the Canadian R.A.F. squadron in the battle of Britain.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his observation. These men are still Canadians, proud of Canada, and most of them want to serve in the air force of their country. I raised this matter with the minister immediately upon my return. At that time I told him that every Canadian in the IR.C.A.F. wanted his brothers in the R.A.F. back in the R.C.A.F. He pointed out the difficulty to me and it was understandable. The RA.F. did not want to lose these very brave and experienced pilots. I was pleased when he announced in the house that the transfer of Canadians in the R.A.F. back to the R.C.A.F. has now been arranged.
I can tell the committee, however, that not all these Canadians will choose to transfer back. A Canadian in the R.A.F. who has a permanent commission can naturally see a little bigger future after the war in the R.A.F. than in the smaller R.CA.F., and there are other Canadians who will want to stay with the RA.F. for sentimental reasons, because of

War Appropriation-Air Services
attachments formed, just as many gallant Americans who joined our R.C.A.F. before the war have chosen to stay with their comrades in the R,C.A.F.
This brings me to the matter of members of the R.C.A.F. attached to the R.A.F. squadrons. The minister brought out clearly that a man who joins the R.C.A.F. in Canada is always a member of the R.C.A.F., irrespective of whether he serves with the R.A.F., with the United States air force, the Australian air force or the South African air force, as some did. He is looked after by this country, promoted by this country and paid by this country. There is, however, a feeling throughout the dominion that the R.C.A.F. Canadians with the R.A.F. squadrons are not getting quite as good a deal as if they were in R.C.A.F. squadrons. That may be owing to'the fact that the R.C.A.F. squadrons naturally have had a little more publicity in this country than the R.A.F. squadrons. However, it is very far from the case, I can assure the committee. I have served in both the R.C.A.F. and the R.A.F., and I think I do know a little about this. The young Canadian who is attached to an R.A.F. squadron does at first feel a little at a loss, perhaps a little strange, and he wishes he were with his own countrymen. If I may be permitted to use a parallel, they are very like the young Canadians who went across to Oxford in peace time as Rhodes scholars. The first year they held together in little groups, did not like the climate, or the English, very much, and were not at all backward about saying so. By the third year, however, they had grown to know and like the English. They yielded to none in their devotion to Oxford. The same is true with respect to these Canadians ini the R.A.F. squadrons. Most of them have a very deep devotion for their squadrons, and I can tell hon. members of an incident that will prove it. The Canadian squadron I was with in Tunisia at one time had several casualties. There were no Canadians immediately available in the reserve pool. We were told we could get Canadians from the adjacent R.A.F. squadrons. It was only with the greatest difficulty that we could get those Canadians to come to the one Canadian squadron out there. I tell the committee and through the committee the mothers of the boys who are with R.A.F. squadrons that they are in the very best of hands.
Another point I should like to mention is the status of R.A.F. airmen in R.C.A.F. squadrons. We have heard all about the R.C.A.F. airmen in the R.A.F. squadrons, but the reverse situation also occurs. There are R.A.F. airmen, Englishmen, Scotsmen and Irishmen, in Canadian squadrons overseas. The reason 100-684
for that is a simple one. Those hon. members who are soldiers from the last war know that the sergeant and the sergeant-major are the real backbone of the fighting forces. We undoubtedly had good men in these ranks in peace time, men with long experience; but with the great expansion that took place these men were naturally commissioned in Canada as officers, and therefore we are very short of long-experienced- and tried senior noncommissioned officers and warrant officers. Such is not the case in the R.A.F., for in the R.A.F. many a good warrant officer cannot afford to take a commission. In the R.C.A.F. a man who takes a commission is financially better off. That is as it should be. In the R.A.F. he drops in financial status, and therefore they have a great number of very experienced senior non-commissioned officers and warrant officers who stay in those ranks. The Canadian squadrons overseas needed men like that. In the squadron I have just left there were two R.A.F. warrant officers, an armourer and a fitter, both with fifteen years in the service. They had served in Britain, in the middle east, and in the far east. One of them had gone to Russia with the Hurricane wing. These men were invaluable. They served with Canadian squadrons and they liked serving with Canadian squadrons, but they serve at R.A.F. rates of pay. In the case of a warrant officer that amounts to the pay of a Canadian corporal.
In the Canadian navy I think they do things better than that. They have the same situation. They have key men of the Royal Navy in our destroyers and corvettes, but they pay them Canadian rates of pay. I may be on the wrong wicket here because I notice the minister said that we pay the full cost of the R.C.A.F. squadrons. Does that include R.C.A.F. pay for those R.A.F. men serving in Canadian squadrons?

speechtext: Frankly, I do not know; I do not think so, because at the time there were R.A.F. commanding officers with our squadrons, I know they were receiving lower pay than officers of a much lower rank.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is quite true.
